questions.q: On which date did the Constitution of India come into force?
questions.a: 26 January 1950

questions.q: The chapter says the Bauddha Saṁghas reflect India's democratic traditions. Who established this monastic community?
questions.a: Gautama Buddha

questions.q: Fig. 6.3 shows the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constitution of India. Who was he?
questions.a: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar

questions.q: Match each event with its date as given in the chapter. 1. The Constituent Assembly was formed 2. The Constitution was adopted 3. The Constitution came into force 4. India attained independence. a. 1947 b. 26 January 1950 c. 1946 d. 26 November 1949
What is democracy, as the chapter recalls it from earlier grades? Name any two principles on which it is founded.
questions.a: Democracy is a form of government in which the source of power and authority lies with the citizens, who elect their representatives through free and fair elections. It is founded on principles such as freedom, equality, justice, rights and duties (any two).
s: Defines democracy: power and authority lie with citizens who elect representatives through free and fair elections
Names any two of freedom, equality, justice, rights, duties

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) Name the three assemblies of the Vedic period that involved collective decision-making. (b) What were the early republican states called? (c) Which three things does the verse from the Aikyamatya Sūktam of the Ṛigveda emphasise?
questions.a: (a) Sabha, Samiti and Vidhata. (b) Gaṇas or saṁghas. (c) Collective thinking, shared discussion and unity of purpose.
s: (a) Sabha, Samiti and Vidhata
(b) Gaṇas or saṁghas
(c) Collective thinking, shared discussion and unity of purpose

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Constituent Assembly drew only on India's own ancient traditions when it made the Constitution. Reason (R): Democratic ideas in India have roots in the Vedic assemblies and the Bauddha Saṁghas. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: The chapter calls the Constitution of India 'robust, flexible, transformative, and responsive'. Which feature described in the chapter best shows that it is flexible?
questions.a: It can evolve through lawful amendments under Article 368 without compromising its fundamental values.
o: It can evolve through lawful amendments under Article 368 without compromising its fundamental values.
It is the world's longest written Constitution.
It took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days to draft.
It guarantees and protects the Fundamental Rights of all citizens.

questions.q: Kabir says, 'India's democracy was copied entirely from Western countries.' Priya replies, 'No, it came entirely from ancient Indian traditions.' Using the chapter, show in three points that each of them is only partly right.
questions.a: (1) Against Kabir: democratic ideas have deep Indian roots, such as the Vedic Sabha, Samiti and Vidhata, the gaṇas or saṁghas, the Bauddha Saṁghas that chose leaders by voting, and the Aikyamatya verse on shared discussion. (2) Against Priya: the chapter says the global spread of democratic values also influenced the Constituent Assembly's Debates. (3) The long struggle for independence revived democratic ideas after foreign rule had limited participation, so the modern Constitution combines indigenous traditions with later developments from around the world.
s: Indian roots named (Vedic assemblies, gaṇas, Bauddha Saṁghas or the Aikyamatya verse), so Kabir is wrong to say 'entirely copied'
Global spread of democratic values influenced the Constituent Assembly Debates, so Priya is wrong to say 'entirely Indian'
Conclusion: the freedom struggle revived these ideas and the Constitution combines both sources

questions.q: Under Universal Adult Franchise in India, a citizen gets the right to vote at what age?
questions.a: 18 years and above

questions.q: What does the idea of popular sovereignty mean?
questions.a: The state derives its authority from the people.
o: The state derives its authority from the people.
The ruler's authority comes from birth in a royal family.
The courts hold final power over every decision of the people.
Only elected representatives, not citizens, hold power.

questions.q: Which Fundamental Right covers Articles 23-24 of the Constitution?
questions.a: Right Against Exploitation

questions.q: True or False: The Right to Education (Article 21A) was added in 2009 and ensures free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14.
questions.a: True. The chapter says Article 21A, the Right to Education, was added in 2009 and ensures free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: Article 21A added in 2009 gives free and compulsory education to children aged 6 to 14

questions.q: What does the Rule of Law establish? Name the two things it ensures.
questions.a: The Rule of Law establishes that no one is above the law. It ensures equality before the law and equal protection of the law.
s: Establishes that no one is above the law
Ensures equality before the law and equal protection of the law

questions.q: Read the statements. I. Equality before law means every individual, irrespective of status, identity or rank, is treated equally by the law. II. The principle of 'procedure established by law' is enshrined in Article 32 of the Constitution. III. Citizens can seek constitutional remedies under Articles 32 and 226 to protect their Fundamental Rights. Which of these are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: In the chapter's list of the six Fundamental Rights with their Articles, which right is the only one linked to a single Article?
questions.a: The Right to Constitutional Remedies

questions.q: Two neighbours quarrel over a boundary wall. The richer one says he will use his influence with local officials to have the other punished. Using the chapter's account of the Rule of Law, explain: (a) where and how this dispute must be settled; (b) why his influence cannot decide it; (c) what the other neighbour is entitled to before any action is taken against him.
questions.a: (a) It must be resolved in a court of law through procedures established by law, not by force or personal influence. (b) Under the Rule of Law no one is above the law and there is equality before the law, so wealth or influence gives him no special power. (c) No citizen can be punished without following the procedure established by law, and he must get a fair opportunity to defend his rights against arbitrary action.
s: (a) Settled in a court of law through procedures established by law, not force or influence
(b) No one is above the law / equality before law, so influence cannot decide
(c) No punishment without procedure established by law; a fair chance to defend his rights

questions.q: A housing society writes election rules for its committee, saying it is borrowing ideas from the Constitution. Rule 1: only members who have paid fees for ten years may vote. Rule 2: votes are cast by raising hands at the meeting. Rule 3: the secretary's family is exempt from fines for late payment. Rule 4: a member accused of breaking a rule is fined only after being told the charge and heard. For each rule, say which principle from the chapter it follows or breaks, and why.
questions.a: Rule 1 breaks the spirit of Universal Adult Franchise, under which every adult citizen votes without extra conditions. Rule 2 breaks the secret ballot that the chapter attaches to the right to vote. Rule 3 breaks the Rule of Law, since equality before the law means no one, whatever their rank, is above the rules. Rule 4 follows the Rule of Law: no one is punished without the procedure established by law and a fair chance to defend oneself.
s: Rule 1 breaks Universal Adult Franchise: every adult votes without added conditions
Rule 2 breaks voting by secret ballot
Rule 3 breaks the Rule of Law / equality before law: no one is above the rules
Rule 4 follows the Rule of Law: procedure and a fair opportunity to defend before punishment

questions.q: Which organ of government interprets the laws?
questions.a: The judiciary

questions.q: How does the chapter define a Public Interest Litigation (PIL)?
questions.a: A legal action initiated in a court of law for the enforcement of public interest.
o: A legal action initiated in a court of law for the enforcement of public interest.
A request to a government office for information under the RTI Act.
A question asked to the government in the first hour of a parliamentary session.
An audit of government accounts by the Comptroller and Auditor General.

questions.q: Match each democratic process with the institution the chapter's table links to it. 1. Electoral process 2. Judicial process 3. Accountability mechanisms 4. Decentralisation. a. Rural and urban local bodies b. CAG, CIC, Lokpal and CVC c. Election Commission of India d. Courts
What is a multi-party system? State one way it helps voters.
questions.a: In a multi-party system several political parties contest elections, representing diverse voices and interests. It gives people the power to choose the party or candidates they consider most suitable.
s: Several political parties contest elections, representing diverse voices and interests
Helps voters: they can choose those they consider most suitable

questions.q: True or False: Political parties in India function within the rules and regulations laid down by the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
questions.a: True. The chapter says political parties function within the framework of rules and regulations laid down by the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the chapter says parties work within the rules of the Representation of the People Act, 1951

questions.q: For each action, name the organ of government that performs it. (a) Parliament passes a new law on road safety. (b) The police and transport department enforce the fines under that law. (c) A High Court declares one clause of the law unconstitutional.
questions.a: (a) The legislature, which makes laws. (b) The executive, which implements laws. (c) The judiciary, which interprets laws and can declare a law inconsistent with the Constitution unconstitutional.
s: (a) Legislature: makes laws
(b) Executive: implements laws
(c) Judiciary: interprets laws and declares an inconsistent law unconstitutional

questions.q: Which pair from the chapter's table of democratic processes is correctly matched with the democratic value it promotes?
questions.a: Federalism: devolution of power

questions.q: Assertion (A): The government must ensure that resources are distributed equitably, especially to the most vulnerable sections of society. Reason (R): Historical factors have led to an unequal distribution of opportunities and resources. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Read the case and answer. A newspaper reports that 46 children of a Scheduled Tribe hamlet have no school within 12 km, and most have stopped studying after Class 5. A social worker, who is not a parent of any of the children, files a case in the High Court asking that the State provide a school. The court hears the case and asks the government to report what it will do. (a) What kind of legal action has the social worker taken, and why can she file it though she is not a parent? (b) Which Article of the Constitution, quoted in the chapter, directs the State to promote the educational interests of the Scheduled Tribes with special care? (c) Which democratic values does the chapter's table link to the judicial process seen here? (d) Why does the chapter say the government must give such groups special attention?
questions.a: (a) A Public Interest Litigation: a legal action in a court for the enforcement of public interest, so it need not be her own private matter. (b) Article 46. (c) Rule of law, equality and justice. (d) Historical factors have caused an unequal distribution of opportunities and resources, so the government must distribute resources equitably, especially to the most vulnerable sections, without discrimination.
s: (a) PIL: a legal action in a court for the enforcement of public interest, not a private matter
(b) Article 46
(c) Rule of law, equality, justice
(d) Historical unequal distribution of opportunities and resources, so equitable distribution to the most vulnerable

questions.q: The chapter names the National Service Scheme (NSS) and the National Cadet Corps (NCC). What are these programmes designed to do?
questions.a: Instil civic responsibility, social awareness and respect for democratic ideals
o: Instil civic responsibility, social awareness and respect for democratic ideals
Train students to conduct elections for the Election Commission
Replace the Gram Sabha as the decision-making body in villages
Check social media posts and remove false ones

questions.q: The chapter defines civil society as voluntary groups, NGOs and community associations that function within society. Which of these is NOT part of civil society?
questions.a: The Election Commission of India
o: A voluntary group that runs a free reading room
An NGO working for clean drinking water

questions.q: In which year did the Right to Information (RTI) Act come into force?
Name two things that newspapers, news channels and social media do in a democracy, according to the chapter.
questions.a: They keep people informed about developments around the world, and they serve as a voice of the masses by raising issues concerning the public and helping resolve them through appropriate mechanisms.
s: Keep people informed about developments around the world
Serve as a voice of the masses: raise public issues and help resolve them

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) Name two habits the chapter suggests for a young citizen to stay well-informed. (b) Name two things that civic responsibility includes, as the chapter's note explains. (c) Name two ways of taking part in democracy shown in Fig. 6.9, 'Youth and Democracy'.
questions.a: (a) Any two: reading newspapers, watching news programmes, using the internet responsibly. (b) Any two: respecting others' rights, using social media responsibly, abiding by laws and rules, appreciating the country's diversity, taking part in activities that strengthen unity. (c) Any two: be media literate, understand the Constitution, follow fundamental duties, take leadership in school and community, participate in nation-building activities such as NCC, NSS and Bharat Scouts and Guides.
s: (a) Two of: reading newspapers, watching news programmes, using the internet responsibly
(b) Two parts of civic responsibility from the note
(c) Two ways from Fig. 6.9

questions.q: Read the statements. I. Civil society organisations, cooperatives and trade unions often adopt democratic decision-making methods. II. Through Public Interest Litigation, campaigns and community organisations, civil society helps make democracy more inclusive and responsive. III. Chaudhary Charan Singh and Babu Jagjivan Ram are named as leaders from rural backgrounds who advocated for the rights of the rural poor. Which of these are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III

questions.q: True or False: According to the chapter, the media's only role in a democracy is to keep people informed about developments around the world.
questions.a: False. Besides keeping people informed, the media serves as a voice of the masses: it raises issues concerning the public and contributes to their resolution, which is why it is called the 'fourth pillar of democracy'.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: it also serves as a voice of the masses, raising public issues and helping resolve them

questions.q: Meena's street has had no working streetlight for three months, although the ward office says money was sanctioned. Suggest three democratic ways, each drawn from the chapter, by which she can get the problem addressed, and say how each one helps.
questions.a: (1) File a request under the RTI Act, 2005 to find out how the sanctioned money was spent; this makes the office accountable. (2) Raise the issue through a newspaper, news channel or responsible social media post; the media acts as a voice of the masses and helps issues get resolved. (3) Take it up with a residents' association or other civil society group, or a local council meeting; civil society acts as a bridge between citizens and the State.
s: RTI request to learn how sanctioned money was used (accountability)
Media raises the issue as a voice of the masses
Civil society group or local council acts as a bridge to the State

questions.q: Consider three ways citizens connect with the State: the media, civil society, and programmes like the NSS and NCC. (a) State what the media does, as the chapter describes it. (b) State what civil society does, with one tool it uses. (c) State what NSS and NCC aim to build in young people. (d) A village has been asking for a road to its school for two years without result. Decide which of the three would help it most. (e) Justify your decision and say why the other two would help less.
questions.a: (a) The media keeps people informed and serves as the voice of the masses, raising public issues and helping resolve them; it is the 'fourth pillar of democracy'. (b) Civil society, meaning voluntary groups, NGOs and community associations, acts as a bridge between citizens and the State through PIL, campaigns and community organisations. (c) Civic responsibility, social awareness and respect for democratic ideals, through community service and teamwork. (d) A reasoned choice, for example civil society. (e) For civil society: it can organise the villagers, run a campaign and, if needed, file a PIL; the media can publicise the issue but cannot itself compel action; NSS and NCC build young citizens' habits and service but are not designed to press a demand on the government. Any choice is accepted if justified with chapter evidence and a comparison with the other two.
s: (a) Media: informs and voices public issues, the fourth pillar
(b) Civil society: voluntary groups, NGOs, associations; uses PIL, campaigns or community organisations
(c) NSS/NCC: civic responsibility, social awareness, respect for democratic ideals
(d) A clear decision on which of the three helps most
(e) Justification from the chapter with a comparison to the other two

questions.q: Which country does the chapter give as an example of direct democracy?
questions.a: Switzerland

questions.q: Which statement describes a presidential democracy, as shown in Fig. 6.4?
questions.a: The executive is independent of the legislature, and the President is elected by the people.
o: The executive is independent of the legislature, and the President is elected by the people.
Members of the executive are also part of the legislature and answer to it.
Citizens directly take part in most decision-making processes.
A monarch is the Head of State and the Prime Minister heads the government.

questions.q: From which Latin word is 'sovereignty' derived, and what does the word mean, as the chapter explains?
questions.a: It comes from the Latin word superanus, meaning 'supreme'. Sovereignty is the supreme, final and independent legal authority of a State over its territory and citizens.
s: Latin superanus, meaning 'supreme'
Supreme, final and independent legal authority of a State over its territory and citizens

questions.q: Using Fig. 6.4 and the chapter's table of countries, name the form of democracy (direct, parliamentary or presidential) in each imaginary country. (a) Country W: citizens gather and vote directly on most decisions. (b) Country X: the people elect a President who heads the executive, which is independent of the legislature. (c) Country Y: the Prime Minister and ministers sit in the legislature and must answer to it. (d) Country Z: a Governor-General appointed by the Monarch is Head of State and a Prime Minister heads the government; name the country in the table it resembles and its form.
questions.a: (a) Direct democracy. (b) Presidential democracy. (c) Parliamentary democracy. (d) It resembles Canada, a parliamentary democracy.
s: (a) Direct democracy
(b) Presidential democracy
(c) Parliamentary democracy
(d) Canada, parliamentary democracy

questions.q: Assertion (A): In a presidential democracy such as the United States of America, the President is accountable to the people. Reason (R): In a presidential democracy, the President is elected by the people. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: In the chapter's table of five countries, which two have a Head of State who is a monarch or is appointed by a monarch?
questions.a: The United Kingdom and Canada
o: India and the United States of America

questions.q: Ritu says, 'India and Canada have the same form of democracy, so their Heads of State hold office in the same way.' Test her claim using the chapter's table. Give one point that supports her, one that does not, and your conclusion.
questions.a: Supports: both are representative, parliamentary democracies with federalism and a multi-party system. Does not support: India's Head of State is the President, while Canada's is a Governor-General appointed by the Monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister. Conclusion: the claim is only partly right; the same form of democracy can have very different Heads of State.
s: Support: both are parliamentary democracies with federalism and multiple parties
Against: India's Head of State is the President; Canada's is a Governor-General appointed by the Monarch on the PM's advice
Conclusion: partly right; same form, different Heads of State

questions.q: A Model Parliament club prepares three fact cards. Card Alpha: a monarch is Head of State, a Prime Minister heads the government, the constitution is unwritten, and there are many parties. Card Beta: a President elected by the people heads an executive independent of the legislature; there is a written constitution with two major parties. Card Gamma: executive power lies with a Federal Council, citizens directly take part in most decisions, and there are several parties. (a) Name the country in the chapter's table that each card describes. (b) Which card's executive is NOT accountable to the legislature? (c) Which card's form would be hardest to follow in a country of over 140 crore people, and why? (d) Name one feature India shares with Alpha and one feature India has that Alpha lacks.
questions.a: (a) Alpha: United Kingdom; Beta: United States of America; Gamma: Switzerland. (b) Beta, because in a presidential democracy the executive is independent of the legislature. (c) Gamma, direct democracy, because the chapter says it is difficult to follow in large countries where citizens cannot all take part directly in most decisions. (d) Shared: both are parliamentary democracies with a Prime Minister heading the government (or multi-party systems). India has a written constitution (or federalism), which Alpha lacks.
s: (a) Alpha UK, Beta USA, Gamma Switzerland
(b) Beta: presidential executive is independent of the legislature
(c) Gamma: direct democracy is difficult in large countries
(d) One shared feature (parliamentary, PM heads government, multi-party) and one India-only feature (written constitution, federalism)

questions.q: According to the chapter, on average about how many people did a Member of Parliament represent in 2019?
questions.a: About 25 lakh

questions.q: Match each item with what the chapter says about women's reservation. 1. Article 243(d) 2. Article 243(t) 3. 21 States and 2 Union Territories 4. 17 States and 1 Union Territory (as of 2023). a. 50% reservation for women in Urban Local Bodies b. Not less than one-third of directly elected seats for women in every Municipality c. 50% reservation for women in Panchayati Raj Institutions d. Not less than one-third of directly elected seats for women in every Panchayat
In the chapter's own words, what makes Indian democracy truly 'living'?
questions.a: Its diversity and citizens' active engagement in the electoral process
o: Its diversity and citizens' active engagement in the electoral process
Its more than one million polling stations
The size of its electorate of nearly a hundred crore voters

questions.q: True or False: Autonomous District Councils are set up in tribal areas of every state of India to preserve tribal customs.
questions.a: False. Autonomous District Councils are established only in specific north-eastern regions, with legislative and judicial authority to preserve tribal customs; tribal areas in other states are covered instead by the PESA Act of 1996, which empowers the Gram Sabha.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: ADCs are only in specific north-eastern regions; PESA (1996) covers tribal areas in other states

questions.q: Read the passage and answer. Kesarpur Gram Panchayat has 27 directly elected seats. Last year it held Special Gram Sabhas on drinking water, kept proper records of every meeting and started Mahila Sabhas, where women of the village discuss their needs before the main Gram Sabha. It also helped set up 12 self-help groups. At the last Gram Sabha, many Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe families spoke for the first time. (a) From the passage, name two steps Kesarpur took that Jethipura Gram Panchayat also took. (b) Whose voice does the Mahila Sabha bring into decision-making? (c) Under Article 243(d), at least how many of Kesarpur's 27 seats must be reserved for women? (d) What does Kesarpur show about democracy beyond elections?
questions.a: (a) Any two: organising Special Gram Sabhas, maintaining proper records, conducting Mahila Sabhas, active participation of SC, ST and women. (b) Women of the village. (c) 27 / 3 = 9 seats. (d) Democracy is not limited to voting: when citizens take an active part in Gram Sabhas and Panchayati Raj institutions, it becomes more responsive, inclusive and effective.
s: (a) Two shared steps: Special Gram Sabhas, proper records, Mahila Sabhas, participation of marginalised groups
(b) Women
(c) 27 / 3 = 9 seats
(d) Democracy goes beyond voting: active participation makes it responsive, inclusive and effective

questions.q: Compare Jethipura Gram Panchayat and South Manubankul Gram Panchayat as described in the chapter's case study. Give one similarity and two differences.
questions.a: Similarity: both are local self-governments that improved people's lives through active participation and were recognised at the national level. Differences: (1) Jethipura is in Sabarkantha, Gujarat, while South Manubankul is in Tripura, within the Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council. (2) Jethipura was recognised with the Nanaji Deshmukh Rashtriya Gaurav Gram Sabha Puraskar in 2019 for conducting Gram Sabhas well and keeping records, while South Manubankul was recognised by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj as a 'women-friendly panchayat' for its focus on women's welfare.
s: Similarity: both improve lives through participation and won national recognition
Difference in location: Gujarat versus Tripura (within an Autonomous District Council)
Difference in focus or recognition: NDRGGSP 2019 for Gram Sabhas and records versus women-friendly panchayat

questions.q: Answer each part in one step. (a) A tribal area lies in a specific north-eastern region. Which body does the chapter say preserves tribal customs there? (b) A student says Indian women, like British women, had to struggle for decades to vote. In which year did women in Britain receive full voting rights, according to the chapter? (c) A voter in Tamil Nadu and a voter in Assam read election material in different languages. In how many scheduled languages does the chapter say Indian elections are conducted? (d) A voter in the village cannot read. What does the chapter say lets her vote independently? (e) A Gram Sabha needs 100 members present for valid proceedings, but only 80 come. Can it take valid decisions? Use the meaning of quorum.
questions.a: (a) The Autonomous District Council. (b) 1928. (c) 22 scheduled languages, along with several other languages. (d) Election symbols. (e) No; quorum is the minimum number of members whose presence makes the proceedings valid, and 80 is below the 100 needed.
s: (a) Autonomous District Council
(c) 22 scheduled languages
(d) Election symbols
(e) No: 80 is below the quorum of 100, so proceedings are not valid

questions.q: An election officer plans polling stations for four places. Island A has 1 voter, forest village B has 250, desert village C has 1,480 and town D has 4,200. Assume each station can serve at most 1,500 voters. (a) How many stations does Island A need, and what does the chapter say about such cases? (b) How many stations does town D need? (c) How many stations are needed in all? (d) The officer notes that candidates from many of India's over 2,800 registered parties may stand. What does the chapter say this large number of parties reflects? (e) A colleague says, 'A station for one voter is a waste of money.' Evaluate this using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 1 station; the chapter says that in some cases polling stations are created even for a single voter. (b) 4,200 / 1,500 = 2.8, so 3 stations. (c) 1 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 6 stations. (d) The country's social and regional diversity, allowing many viewpoints to compete peacefully. (e) The colleague is wrong by the chapter's standard: India's democracy stands out for its scale, depth and inclusiveness, setting up over one million stations even in remote mountains, forests, deserts and islands; every citizen's vote counts equally, so the cost is justified to keep the right to vote real for all.
s: (a) 1 station; stations are set up even for a single voter
(c) 1 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 6 stations
(d) Social and regional diversity; many viewpoints compete peacefully
(e) Reject the claim: inclusiveness and equal vote of every citizen justify the station

questions.q: Who led the mass movements against the Emergency and was popularly known as Lok Nayak?
questions.a: Jayaprakash Narayan

questions.q: Assertion (A): During the Emergency of 1975-77, citizens' freedom was restricted. Reason (R): During this period a majority of Fundamental Rights were suspended and the press was censored. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Read the statements about the Emergency. I. In June 1975, a National Emergency was imposed on the grounds of external aggression. II. During the Emergency, the press was censored and numerous political leaders and activists were arrested. III. The Emergency was lifted in 1977, and general elections were held. Which of these are correct?
questions.a: II and III only

questions.q: (a) A group of students cleans the local park and reports a broken water pipe to the ward office. (b) Another student scratches a bus seat and forwards a rumour without checking it. For each, say whether it strengthens or weakens democratic values, with the chapter's reason.
questions.a: (a) Strengthens: democracy is reflected in everyday behaviour and civic responsibility, and taking interest in public issues is the opposite of the indifference that harms democracy. (b) Weakens: the chapter says damaging public property and spreading misinformation weaken democratic values.
s: (a) Strengthens: civic responsibility and interest in public issues
(b) Weakens: damaging public property and spreading misinformation weaken democratic values

questions.q: Read the case and answer. Ward 9 of Lakhanpur has 3,000 adult voters, but only 1,350 voted in the last municipal election. A survey of the non-voters found that 40% of them said, 'Nothing ever changes, so why bother?' Many women said family elders stopped them from attending ward meetings. Two days before polling, a message on social media falsely claimed that the polling date had been shifted. (a) What percentage of the voters voted, and how many non-voters said 'nothing ever changes'? (b) Which challenges from the chapter does the 'nothing ever changes' reply reflect? (c) Which challenge does the women's experience show? (d) Which challenge does the false message show, and what harm does the chapter say it can do?
questions.a: (a) 1,350 / 3,000 x 100 = 45%; non-voters = 3,000 - 1,350 = 1,650, and 40% of 1,650 = 660. (b) Indifference towards public issues, which harms the health of democracy, and reduced public trust caused by gaps in implementing laws and policies. (c) Gender inequality and social prejudices that act as barriers to equal participation. (d) Misinformation or fake news spread through social media; it can influence public opinion, create confusion and sometimes even lead to conflict.
s: (a) 45% voted; 40% of 1,650 non-voters = 660
(b) Indifference to public issues and low trust from gaps in implementation
(c) Gender inequality / social prejudice as a barrier to participation
(d) Misinformation/fake news: influences opinion, creates confusion, may lead to conflict

questions.q: Arjun says, 'The Constitution guarantees our rights, so citizens need do nothing more to protect democracy.' Using the chapter's account of challenges and of the Emergency, show in three points why this is wrong.
questions.a: (1) The chapter says the Constitution, while guaranteeing rights, also expects citizens to exercise them responsibly; democracy needs constant care, awareness and active participation. (2) During the Emergency of 1975-77 most Fundamental Rights were suspended despite the Constitution; mass movements led by Jayaprakash Narayan and the people's vote in 1977 helped restore democracy. (3) Indifference, misinformation and actions like damaging public property weaken democracy, so constitutional safeguards work only together with informed, active citizens.
s: Constitution expects rights to be used responsibly; democracy needs constant care and participation
Emergency: rights were suspended; citizens' movements and the 1977 vote restored democracy
Indifference and misinformation weaken democracy, so safeguards need active citizens

questions.q: Your school wants to reduce the spread of fake news among students and is choosing among three plans. Plan A: ban all phones and news apps on the campus. Plan B: start a media-literacy club where students learn to check the source of a message before sharing it. Plan C: punish any student who shares a false message, without discussion. Evaluate each plan using the chapter, and recommend one.
questions.a: Plan A cuts students off from news and the internet, which the chapter says help young citizens stay informed, so it weakens informed participation. Plan B builds media literacy, shown in Fig. 6.9, and the responsible use of social media that is part of civic responsibility, so it tackles misinformation at its source. Plan C may scare students but does not teach them to judge information, and punishing without a hearing goes against fair procedure. Recommendation: Plan B, because access to authentic information and responsible use of media strengthen democracy.
s: Plan A judged: cuts off access to information the chapter says citizens need
Plan B judged: builds media literacy and responsible social media use
Plan C judged: does not teach judgement; punishment without hearing is unfair
Recommends Plan B with a chapter-based reason

questions.q: Plan a one-month 'Democracy in Action' programme for your Class 9. (a)-(d) Describe four activities, each linked to a different way of participating shown in Fig. 6.9 or the 'Think, Discuss, Act' box, and say which challenge from the chapter (illiteracy, misinformation, inequality, indifference) each one meets. (e) Say which activity you expect to do the most to strengthen democracy, and justify it.
questions.a: A sample answer: (a) A fact-check corner where students verify viral messages before sharing (be media literate; meets misinformation). (b) Reading a few Fundamental Rights and Duties aloud each week with discussion (understand the Constitution and follow fundamental duties; meets indifference). (c) Students teach elderly neighbours to read election symbols and notices (take leadership in the community; meets illiteracy). (d) An NSS-style drive inviting girls and boys equally to lead class committees (nation-building activities and leadership; meets gender inequality). (e) For example, the fact-check corner, because the chapter names fake news on social media as a major recent concern that can create confusion and even conflict. Any four relevant, distinct activities with correct links and a justified choice earn the marks.
s: (a) Activity linked to a Fig. 6.9 way and a named challenge
(b) Second distinct activity with correct links
(c) Third distinct activity with correct links
(d) Fourth distinct activity with correct links
(e) Chooses the most effective activity and justifies it from the chapter
